mainTopic: A worker's travel time, a דרשה on תהלים 104, and the story of רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון arresting thieves for the government
overview: ריש לקיש teaches that a פועל walks home from work on his own time, but walks out to work on the בעל הבית's time, learning it from a פסוק in תהלים. The גמרא asks why a פסוק is needed when local custom decides. It answers that the rule is for a brand-new city, for workers gathered from many towns, or for an employer who hired 'by Torah law.' Next comes a דרשה on the same chapter of תהלים: night is this world, where the רשעים roam like forest animals, and sunrise is עולם הבא, where the צדיקים receive their reward. This leads to a story. רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון teaches an officer how to recognize thieves, and the government then appoints him to do the job himself. רבי יהושע בן קרחה rebukes him as 'vinegar son of wine' for handing Jews over to be killed. After רבי אלעזר has an insolent laundryman executed, he regrets it, until he learns the man was truly wicked. To be sure he is righteous, he has his belly opened, and even the red veins in his fat do not rot. The amud ends as a similar story begins about רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי.

steps.title: Travel home is on the worker's time; travel to work is on the employer's time
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש rules that a פועל's trip home comes out of his own time, while his trip out to work comes out of the בעל הבית's time, based on a פסוק in תהלים.
steps.simpleTranslation: A worker's coming home is on his own time. His going out to work is on the employer's time. As it says: 'The sun rises, they slink away and lie down in their dens. Man goes out to his work and to his labor until evening.'
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש gives a rule about a worker's travel time. He proves it from a פסוק that says people go out to work when the sun rises and keep working until evening.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says a person 'goes out' only after sunrise, so the walk to work in the morning is part of the paid day. It also says he works 'until evening', so he must work right up to nightfall and walk home on his own time afterward.

keyTerms.meaning: In his coming in, meaning returning home from the field
In his going out, meaning heading out to work
The employer, the owner who hired him

steps.confusionAlert: 'Coming in' and 'going out' are about walking between the town and the field. Coming in is the evening walk home, and going out is the morning walk to work.

phrases.english: A worker, in his coming in, is on his own [time];
phrases.notes: 'Coming in' means walking home at the end of the day.

phrases.english: in his going out, it is on the employer's [time],
as it is stated:
"The sun rises, they slink away
and lie down in their dens.
Man goes out to his work
and to his labor until evening."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues ריש לקיש's statement, which follows the משנה about workers' hours.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The worker's walk home comes out of his own time. His walk to work comes out of the employer's time. The source is תהלים 104:22–23.

steps.title: Why not just follow local custom?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges ריש לקיש: the משנה says local custom decides work hours, so why do we need a פסוק?
steps.simpleTranslation: But let us just see what the custom is there!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges ריש לקיש's rule. Since work hours follow local custom, a פסוק should not be needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If every place follows its own custom, a rule from the תורה seems pointless. The challenge forces the גמרא to find a case where there is no custom to follow.

keyTerms.meaning: Let us see, let us check

phrases.english: But let us see how they are accustomed [to do]!
phrases.notes: This points back to the משנה, which says workers' hours follow the custom of the place.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the need for ריש לקיש's rule.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Work terms follow local custom, so a פסוק-based rule seems unnecessary.

steps.title: A new city with no custom yet
steps.stepSummary: The rule applies in a brand-new city that has no custom yet.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is talking about a new city.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that ריש לקיש means a brand-new city, where no custom has formed yet.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With no local custom to follow, we need a default rule, and the פסוק supplies it. This narrows ריש לקיש's rule to a specific situation.

keyTerms.meaning: A new city that has no custom yet

phrases.english: In a new city.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 2.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Every place has a custom, so the פסוק is unneeded.
steps.terutzMaskana: In a new city there is no custom, so the תורה's default applies.

steps.title: Why not follow the workers' hometown custom?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back: even in a new city, check where the workers came from and follow that town's custom.
steps.simpleTranslation: Then let us see where they came from!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer. Even in a new city, the workers came from somewhere, so follow the custom of their hometown.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Workers in a new city still bring their old customs with them. So the new-city answer alone does not fully explain why a default rule is needed.

phrases.english: But let us see where they came from!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 3.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The workers' original town has a custom that could be followed.

steps.title: A mixed group from many towns
steps.stepSummary: The workers were gathered from many different towns, so there is no single custom to follow.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is talking about a mixed group.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the workers came from many places with different customs, so no one custom applies.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without one shared custom, we need a default rule again, and the פסוק provides it.

keyTerms.meaning: A mixed group gathered from many places

phrases.english: With a gathered, mixed group.
phrases.notes: Literally 'gathered ones': workers collected from many different towns.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 4.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The workers' hometown custom would decide.
steps.terutzMaskana: The workers came from many towns, so there is no single custom and the פסוק decides.

steps.title: The employer hired them 'by Torah law'
steps.stepSummary: A different answer: the employer told the workers he was hiring them on the terms of a תורה-law worker.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you want, say instead: he told them, 'You are hired by me like a worker by Torah law.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second, different answer to the challenge. ריש לקיש is describing the terms that apply when the employer hires 'by Torah law.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here we do not need a place without a custom. The employer chose the תורה's terms himself, so ריש לקיש is just telling us what those terms are.

keyTerms.meaning: If you want, say: introduces another answer
A worker by Torah law, on the תורה's default terms

steps.whatToRemember: ריש לקיש's rule is the תורה's default. It applies when there is no custom to follow, or when the employer hired 'by Torah law.'
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that local custom normally decides, and the תורה's rule is the fallback.

phrases.english: If you want, say:
that he said to them:
"You are hired by me like a worker by Torah law."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives another answer to the challenge of step 2.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Custom always decides, so the פסוק is pointless.
steps.terutzMaskana: The employer chose the תורה's terms, and ריש לקיש spells them out.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The פסוק-based rule is the תורה's default for workers.

steps.title: Night is this world; wild animals are the wicked
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא (or רב יוסף) explains a nearby פסוק: the darkness is this world, and the forest animals that creep out are the רשעים.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא taught, and some say רב יוסף taught: What does the פסוק 'You make darkness and it is night, in which all the forest animals creep' mean? 'Darkness and night' is this world, which is like night. 'All the forest animals creep' means the wicked in it, who are like wild animals in a forest.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now moves from the halacha to a דרשה on the same chapter of תהלים. It reads the night in the פסוק as this world and the forest animals as the רשעים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just as wild animals roam freely at night, the wicked seem to roam freely and have power in this world. This sets up the next פסוק, where sunrise will stand for the next world.

keyTerms.meaning: Explained a פסוק in a deeper, homiletic way

phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira expounded,
and some say Rav Yosef taught:
What is that which is written:
"You make darkness and it is night,
phrases.notes: תהלים 104:20

phrases.english: in which all the animals of the forest creep"?
"You make darkness and it is night":
this is this world, which is like night.
"In which all the animals of the forest creep":
these are the wicked in it,
who are like an animal in the forest.

steps.triggerLanguage: דָּרֵשׁ רַבִּי זֵירָא וְאָמְרִי לַהּ תָּנֵי רַב יוֹסֵף
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from ריש לקיש's halacha to an aggadic reading of the same chapter of תהלים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Night in the פסוק is this world, and the roaming forest animals are the רשעים.

steps.title: Sunrise for the righteous, גיהנם for the wicked
steps.stepSummary: The דרשה continues: the sun rises for the צדיקים, the רשעים are gathered into גיהנם, and every צדיק gets a dwelling fitting his honor.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'The sun rises, they slink away and lie down in their dens.' 'The sun rises' for the righteous. 'They slink away': the wicked go to גיהנם. 'And lie down in their dens': every single righteous person has a dwelling place that fits his honor.
steps.whatsHappening: The דרשה continues with the next פסוק. Sunrise stands for the reward of the צדיקים, and the wicked are swept away to גיהנם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the night of this world the wicked roamed free. When the 'sun' of the next world rises, it shines for the צדיקים and the wicked are 'gathered away'. The 'dens' are read as each צדיק's own place, matched to his level.

phrases.english: "The sun rises, they slink away
phrases.notes: Night was this world, so the sunrise here points to the next world.

phrases.english: and lie down in their dens."
"The sun rises": for the righteous;
"they slink away": the wicked [go] to Gehenna;
"and lie down in their dens":
you have no righteous person at all
who does not have a dwelling fitting his honor.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the דרשה from night (this world) to sunrise (עולם הבא).
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In עולם הבא the צדיקים shine, the רשעים go to גיהנם, and each צדיק gets a place fitting his honor.

steps.title: The righteous go out to receive their reward
steps.stepSummary: 'Man goes out to his work' means the צדיקים go out to get their reward. 'Until evening' refers to one who finished his work before the evening of his life.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Man goes out to his work': the righteous go out to receive their reward. 'And to his labor until evening': this is about someone who finished his work by evening.
steps.whatsHappening: The דרשה ends with the same words ריש לקיש used for workers. Here they are read as the צדיקים collecting their reward for a life of work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'work' becomes the reward for one's labor, like a worker getting his wages. 'Until evening' teaches that the reward goes to someone who completed his task before his life ended.

keyTerms.meaning: Evening, here hinting at the end of life

steps.whatToRemember: The same פסוק teaches two things. In halacha, a worker works until evening. In aggadah, a צדיק who finishes his life's work 'by evening' goes out to receive his reward in עולם הבא.

phrases.english: "Man goes out to his work":
the righteous go out to receive their reward;
"and to his labor until evening":
about one who completed his work by evening.
phrases.notes: 'Evening' here hints at the end of a person's life: he finished his work before it ended.

steps.triggerLanguage: יֵצֵא אָדָם לְפׇעֳלוֹ יֵצְאוּ צַדִּיקִים לְקַבֵּל שְׂכָרָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the דרשה with the next פסוק (תהלים 104:23).
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The צדיקים receive their reward, specifically one who completed his work before the 'evening' of his life.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר challenges the officer: how do you know you have the right people?
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון meets an officer who arrests thieves. He asks how he can catch them, since the פסוק compares them to hidden animals. Maybe he is arresting צדיקים and letting the רשעים go free.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר son of רבי שמעון met an officer who arrested thieves. He asked him: How can you catch them? They are like wild animals that hide, as the פסוק says, 'in it all the beasts of the forest creep.' Some say he quoted a different פסוק: 'He lies in wait in hiding like a lion in his den.' Maybe you are catching good people and letting the wicked go!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a story. רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון challenges an officer whose job is to catch thieves.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 7 explained that the 'forest animals' in the פסוק are the רשעים. רבי אלעזר uses this idea: wicked people are sneaky and hide in the dark like animals. So an officer could easily make mistakes, arresting innocent people while the real thieves escape.

keyTerms.meaning: An officer or policeman of the government

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon
found a certain officer
who was arresting thieves.
He said to him: How are you able to catch them?
Aren't they compared to wild animals,
as it is written: "In it all the beasts of the forest creep"?
phrases.notes: תהלים 104:20, the same פסוק explained back in step 7.

phrases.aramaic: אִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי מֵהַאי קְרָא קָאָמַר לֵיהּ:
phrases.english: Some say he said it to him from this verse:
"He lies in wait in hiding like a lion in his den."
phrases.notes: תהלים 10:9

phrases.english: Perhaps you are taking the righteous
and leaving the wicked?

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן אַשְׁכַּח לְהָהוּא פַּרְהַגְוָנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds a story on the פסוק explained in steps 7 to 9, using the idea that the 'forest animals' are the רשעים.
steps.kashyaTarget: The officer's ability to arrest the right people
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Wicked people hide like animals in the dark, so the officer cannot reliably tell them apart and may punish the innocent.

steps.title: The officer answers that it is the king's order
steps.stepSummary: The officer replies that he has no choice. The king commanded him to catch thieves.
steps.simpleTranslation: The officer said: What can I do? It is the king's order.
steps.whatsHappening: The officer answers רבי אלעזר's challenge. He is not free to stop, because this is a royal command.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The officer does not deny the problem. He only explains that he cannot quit the job. This opens the door for רבי אלעזר to offer a better method in the next step.

phrases.english: He said to him: And what shall I do?
It is the king's order.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to רבי אלעזר's challenge by explaining that the officer has no choice.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The officer should stop, since he might be arresting innocent people.
steps.terutzMaskana: He cannot stop, because the king ordered it. The real question becomes how to do the job correctly.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר teaches a test: look for the man dozing in the tavern
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר tells the officer to go to the tavern at the fourth hour of the day. If he sees someone dozing over his wine, he should ask who that person is.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: Come, I will teach you what to do. Go into the tavern at the fourth hour of the day. If you see a man drinking wine with a cup in his hand and dozing off, ask about him.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר starts giving the officer a method for finding real thieves. This step sets up the test, and the next step explains how to judge the answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The fourth hour is still early in the day. Someone falling asleep then was probably awake during the night. The officer must now find out why.

phrases.english: He said: Come, I will teach you how to do it.
Go in at the fourth hour to the tavern.

phrases.aramaic: כִּי חָזֵית אִינִישׁ דְּקָא שָׁתֵי חַמְרָא
phrases.english: When you see a person drinking wine
and holding a cup in his hand
and dozing, ask about him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Since the officer must keep working, רבי אלעזר offers a way to identify thieves more accurately.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A man dozing over wine early in the day should be investigated, since he was likely awake at night.

steps.title: How to judge the dozing man: scholar, worker, night worker, or thief
steps.stepSummary: If the dozing man is a Torah scholar, he got up early to learn. If he is a worker, he got up early to work. If he works at night, his work is quiet. If none of these fits, he is a thief.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he is a young Torah scholar, he got up early to learn. If he is a worker, he got up early to do his job. If his work is at night, he does quiet work, like thinning metal. If none of these, he is a thief, so arrest him.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר finishes his test. He lists the innocent reasons a person might be tired, and says that anyone left over is a thief.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The method works by ruling out every honest reason for being tired in the morning. Only after the innocent explanations are excluded may the officer assume the man was up all night stealing.

keyTerms.meaning: He beats metal thin, a quiet kind of work

steps.whatToRemember: The test assumes a person is innocent until every honest reason for being tired has been ruled out.

phrases.english: If he is a young Torah scholar and is dozing,
he got up early for his learning.
phrases.notes: Read the word as קַדּוֹמֵי. The א in front looks like a printed reference mark, not part of the word.

phrases.aramaic: אִי פּוֹעֵל הוּא – קָדֵים קָא עָבֵיד עֲבִידְתֵּיהּ,
phrases.english: If he is a worker, he got up early and did his work.
And if his work is at night, he was thinning metal.
phrases.notes: That kind of work makes no noise, so nobody would have heard him working at night.

phrases.english: And if not, he is a thief, and arrest him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how to evaluate the dozing man described in step 12.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Rule out scholars, day workers, and quiet night workers. Anyone else who is dozing is presumed to be a thief.

steps.title: The king appoints רבי אלעזר himself to catch thieves
steps.stepSummary: The king's court hears of רבי אלעזר's advice and decides that he should carry it out. He is appointed and begins arresting thieves.
steps.simpleTranslation: The matter was heard in the king's palace. They said: The one who read the letter should be the one to deliver it. They brought רבי אלעזר son of רבי שמעון, and he went around arresting thieves.
steps.whatsHappening: The story takes a turn. Because רבי אלעזר came up with the method, the government makes him the one to use it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The saying about the 'reader of the letter' means that whoever suggests a plan should carry it out. רבי אלעזר now goes from adviser to actual officer. This sets up the rebuke in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: The king's house, the royal court

phrases.english: The matter was heard in the king's house.
They said: The reader of the letter
should himself be its messenger.
They brought Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon,
and he went on arresting thieves.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows the result of רבי אלעזר's advice: he is now appointed to apply it himself.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון becomes a government agent who arrests thieves.

steps.title: רבי יהושע בן קרחה rebukes him: vinegar son of wine
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן קרחה sends רבי אלעזר a harsh message. He calls him vinegar, the son of wine, and asks how long he will hand over the Jewish people to be killed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהושע בן קרחה sent him a message: Vinegar, son of wine! How long will you hand over the people of our God to be killed?
steps.whatsHappening: Another חכם attacks רבי אלעזר for working for the government. He says that by catching Jews for the king, רבי אלעזר is sending them to their deaths.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Vinegar is wine that has gone sour. Calling him 'vinegar son of wine' means he has fallen far below his great father, רבי שמעון. The complaint is that a Jew should not hand fellow Jews over to a non-Jewish government that will execute them.

keyTerms.meaning: Vinegar, son of wine: a lesser son of a great father
Handing over, informing on someone to the authorities

steps.confusionAlert: רבי יהושע בן קרחה is not saying the thieves are innocent. His complaint is that רבי אלעזר is handing Jews over to a non-Jewish government to be killed.
steps.whyThisMatters: This rebuke raises the serious issue of a Jew handing over fellow Jews to non-Jewish authorities, even when they really are guilty.

phrases.aramaic: שְׁלַח לֵיהּ רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן קׇרְחָה
phrases.english: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha sent to him:
Vinegar, son of wine!
phrases.notes: Vinegar is spoiled wine. He means: you have turned out much worse than your great father, רבי שמעון.

phrases.english: Until when will you hand over
the people of our God to be killed?

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁלַח לֵיהּ רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן קׇרְחָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds critically to רבי אלעזר's new role as a thief-catcher for the king.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון's work arresting thieves for the government
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Handing Jews over to a non-Jewish government that executes them is improper, and it makes him unworthy of his righteous father.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר defends himself: removing thorns from the vineyard
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר בר רבי שמעון answers רבי יהושע בן קרחה that he is only removing wicked people from the Jewish people.
steps.simpleTranslation: He sent back to him: I am removing thorns from the vineyard.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר answers the harsh message from Step 15. He says he is not hurting the Jewish people. He is cleaning out the wicked among them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהושע בן קרחה said that רבי אלעזר was handing Jews over to death. רבי אלעזר reframes it: the thieves are like thorns that harm the vineyard, so removing them helps the vineyard. He is presenting his work as a service to the people, not a betrayal.

keyTerms.meaning: Thorns, a picture of wicked people
Vineyard, a picture of the Jewish people

phrases.english: He sent to him:
phrases.notes: This is רבי אלעזר answering רבי יהושע בן קרחה.

phrases.english: I am removing thorns from the vineyard.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁלַח לֵיהּ: קוֹצִים אֲנִי מְכַלֶּה מִן הַכֶּרֶם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the attack in Step 15
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reframing: the act is removing harm, not causing harm
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Arresting Jews means handing the Jewish people over to death
steps.terutzMaskana: Arresting thieves cleans the people of wicked members

steps.title: Let the Owner of the vineyard remove His own thorns
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן קרחה rejects the answer: removing the wicked is God's job, not yours.
steps.simpleTranslation: He sent back to him: Let the Owner of the vineyard come and remove His thorns.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע בן קרחה pushes back on רבי אלעזר's answer. He does not say the thieves are innocent. He says it is not רבי אלעזר's place to punish them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He accepts the picture of thorns and a vineyard but uses it against רבי אלעזר. The vineyard has an Owner, and only He should decide which thorns to remove. The objection moves from whether the thieves are wicked to who has the right to remove them.

keyTerms.meaning: The Owner of the vineyard, meaning ה׳

phrases.english: He sent to him:
Let the owner of the vineyard come
phrases.notes: The Owner of the vineyard means ה׳.

phrases.english: and remove His thorns.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁלַח לֵיהּ: יָבֹא בַּעַל הַכֶּרֶם וִיכַלֶּה אֶת קוֹצָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the defense given in Step 16
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects רבי אלעזר's justification for his role
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Even if the thieves are wicked, punishing them belongs to ה׳ and not to a person working for the government

steps.title: The laundryman insults רבי אלעזר and is arrested
steps.stepSummary: A laundryman calls רבי אלעזר 'vinegar son of wine.' He decides the man must be wicked and has him arrested.
steps.simpleTranslation: One day a certain laundryman met him and called him 'vinegar son of wine.' He said: Since he is so brazen, he must be a wicked man. He told the officers: Seize him. They seized him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new story. A laundryman insults רבי אלעזר, and רבי אלעזר has him arrested because the insult shows how brazen the man is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The laundryman uses the same insult רבי יהושע בן קרחה had used. רבי אלעזר reasons that someone this brazen toward a Torah scholar is likely a wicked person. His arrest is based on a guess, not on proof, and that sets up the rest of the story.

keyTerms.meaning: Vinegar son of wine: a bad son of a great father

phrases.aramaic: יוֹמָא חַד פְּגַע בֵּיהּ הָהוּא כּוֹבֵס,
phrases.english: One day a certain laundryman met him,
he called him "vinegar son of wine."
phrases.notes: This is the same insult רבי יהושע בן קרחה used back in Step 15.

phrases.english: He said: since he is so brazen,
learn from this that he is a wicked man.
He said to them: Seize him.
They seized him.

steps.triggerLanguage: יוֹמָא חַד פְּגַע בֵּיהּ הָהוּא כּוֹבֵס
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new episode that tests רבי אלעזר's judgment
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי אלעזר judges the laundryman as wicked because of his brazenness and has him arrested

steps.title: רבי אלעזר regrets, fails to save him, and weeps at the gallows
steps.stepSummary: After calming down, רבי אלעזר tries to free the laundryman but cannot. The man is hanged, and רבי אלעזר cries.
steps.simpleTranslation: After his mind calmed, he went after him to redeem him, but he could not. He read about him: 'Whoever guards his mouth and tongue guards his soul from troubles.' They hanged him. He stood under the gallows and wept.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר feels he acted too fast and tries to undo it, but it is too late. He stands crying at the execution.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His arrest was made in anger, and now he is not sure it was right. The פסוק he quotes says the man brought this on himself with his words. Still, his crying shows he feels responsible, which sets up the comfort in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: To redeem him, to get him freed

phrases.english: After his mind calmed down,
he went after him to redeem him
but he was not able to.
He read about him:
"Whoever guards his mouth and his tongue
guards his soul from troubles."
phrases.notes: משלי 21:23

phrases.english: They hanged him.
He stood under the gallows and wept.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְבָתַר דְּנָח דַּעְתֵּיהּ אֲזַל בָּתְרֵיהּ לְפָרוֹקֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows the result of the arrest in Step 18 and רבי אלעזר's regret
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי אלעזר could not undo his arrest. The man was executed, and רבי אלעזר grieved.

steps.title: They comfort him: the laundryman was truly wicked
steps.stepSummary: People tell רבי אלעזר not to feel bad, because the laundryman and his son had sinned with a betrothed girl on יום הכפורים.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: רבי, do not feel bad, for he and his son had relations with a betrothed girl on יום הכפורים.
steps.whatsHappening: The people standing there answer רבי אלעזר's worry. The man he condemned really was deeply wicked.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלעזר feared he had caused an innocent man's death. The people reveal that the man had committed a sin punishable by death, and on the holiest day. This shows that his guess in Step 18 was correct.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it not be bad in your eyes; do not feel bad
The Day of Atonement, the holiest day of the year

phrases.english: They said to him: Rabbi,
let it not be bad in your eyes
for he and his son had relations with a betrothed girl
on Yom Kippur.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ: רַבִּי, אַל יֵרַע בְּעֵינֶיךָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the grief shown in Step 19
steps.terutzResolutionType: New information that justifies the outcome
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The laundryman may have been innocent, so his death was a wrong
steps.terutzMaskana: The laundryman was truly wicked, so רבי אלעזר's judgment was right

steps.title: If his guesses are right, his certainties surely are
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר rejoices and makes a קל וחומר: if even his suspicions were accurate, his sure judgments must be accurate too. He is confident his body will not decay.
steps.simpleTranslation: He put his hand on his belly and said: Rejoice, my innards, rejoice! If your doubts are this accurate, your certainties are surely even more so. I am sure about you that maggot and worm will not have power over you.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר learns from the laundryman story that his judgment can be trusted. He takes this as proof that his arrests of thieves are correct.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He uses a קל וחומר: the laundryman was arrested on a mere guess, and even that turned out right. His arrests of thieves are based on clearer signs, so they are surely right. He sees this as a sign that he is righteous and that his body will not rot after death.

keyTerms.meaning: All the more so (a קל וחומר)
Maggot and worm, which eat a body after death

steps.whatToRemember: The laundryman story becomes רבי אלעזר's proof: a correct guess shows that his certain judgments are surely correct.

phrases.english: He placed his hand on his innards
and said: Rejoice, my innards, rejoice!
If your doubts turn out like this,

phrases.aramaic: וַדָּאוֹת שֶׁלָּכֶם – עַל אַחַת כַּמָּה וְכַמָּה.
phrases.english: your certainties are all the more so.
I am assured about you
that maggot and worm will not rule over you.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמָה סְפֵיקוֹת שֶׁלָּכֶם כָּךְ וַדָּאוֹת שֶׁלָּכֶם עַל אַחַת כַּמָּה וְכַמָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a conclusion from the news in Step 20
steps.raayaObject: That רבי אלעזר's arrests of thieves are correct and that he is righteous
steps.raayaSupportSource: A קל וחומר from the laundryman, whose wickedness was confirmed even though he was arrested on a guess

steps.title: The surgery: his fat does not rot in the summer sun
steps.stepSummary: Still uneasy, רבי אלעזר is put to sleep and his belly is cut open. Baskets of fat are left in the hot sun of תמוז and אב and do not rot.
steps.simpleTranslation: Even so, his mind was not settled. They gave him a sleeping potion, brought him into a marble house, and cut open his belly. They took out basket after basket of fat, placed them in the sun in תמוז and אב, and it did not rot.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר is still not at peace, so he tests himself in a dramatic way. The fat from his body does not rot, which confirms that he is righteous.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His reasoning in Step 21 was not enough to calm him, so he wanted a physical sign. Things left in the sun in the hottest months normally spoil. Because his fat did not rot, this was taken as proof that his judgments were right, and the next step questions whether that proves anything.

keyTerms.meaning: A marble house, where surgery was done

steps.whatToRemember: רבי אלעזר looked for a physical sign of his righteousness: his fat did not rot even in the summer sun. The next steps test whether this is really a sign.

phrases.english: Even so, his mind was not settled.
They gave him a sleeping potion to drink
and brought him into a marble house
and cut open his belly.
They were taking out of it
basket after basket of fat
and placing them in the sun in Tammuz and Av
phrases.notes: תמוז and אב are the hottest summer months, when things spoil fastest.

phrases.english: and it did not rot.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes beyond the reasoning of Step 21 with a physical test
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The fat that did not rot confirmed that רבי אלעזר was righteous and that his judgments were correct.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון was righteous and his judgments in arresting thieves were correct
steps.raayaSupportSource: A physical test: fat from his belly did not rot in the sun of תמוז and אב

steps.title: Fat never rots, so what was proven?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the proof from the last step: fat does not rot anyway, so the fresh fat proves nothing special.
steps.simpleTranslation: But all fat does not rot anyway!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the proof from step 22. If fat naturally does not rot, then fat staying fresh in the sun is no sign that רבי אלעזר was righteous.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 22 treated the unrotting fat as a miracle that showed רבי אלעזר judged correctly. This challenge says that is just how fat behaves. If that is true, the 'sign' is not really a sign.

keyTerms.meaning: Fat (the fat taken out of his belly)

phrases.english: All fat also
does not rot!
phrases.notes: Two spellings of the same word for 'rot'; the word in square brackets is the corrected wording.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the sign described in step 22
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the unrotting fat proved רבי אלעזר's righteousness
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Fat naturally does not rot, so its staying fresh proves nothing.

steps.title: The red veins should have rotted, but they did not
steps.stepSummary: Plain fat may not rot, but the red veins inside it do. Here even the red veins stayed fresh, so it really was a sign.
steps.simpleTranslation: Fat by itself may not rot, but when it has red veins in it, it rots. Here, even though there were red veins, it did not rot.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. The miracle was not about plain fat. It was about the red veins inside the fat, which normally do rot, staying fresh.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer agrees that pure fat does not rot. But it points to something in the fat that should have rotted: the red veins. Because even those stayed fresh in the heat of תמוז and אב, the proof from step 22 stands.

keyTerms.meaning: Red veins / red streaks inside the fat

steps.confusionAlert: The answer does not say that fat normally rots. It agrees that plain fat stays fresh. The miracle was that the red veins inside it, which do rot, did not.

phrases.english: All fat (does not rot),
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the words in round brackets.

phrases.english: [when it has] red veins, it rots.
phrases.notes: The words in square brackets are added in the corrected wording.

phrases.english: Here, even though
there were red veins,
it did not rot.

steps.triggerLanguage: כֹּל תַּרְבָּא כִּי אִית בֵּהּ שֻׁרְיָקֵי סֻמָּקֵי מַסְרַח
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 23
steps.terutzResolutionType: Making the case more specific: the sign was the red veins, not the plain fat
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Fat never rots, so its staying fresh is not a sign.
steps.terutzMaskana: Red veins in fat do rot. Their staying fresh was a real sign.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר applies a verse about his flesh to himself
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר reads the פסוק 'My flesh also dwells in safety' about himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: He read about himself: 'My flesh also dwells in safety.'
steps.whatsHappening: The story of רבי אלעזר ends. He applies a פסוק from תהלים to himself, since his flesh truly stayed safe from rotting.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק matches what happened: his flesh did not decay. It seals his confidence from step 21 that his judgments were correct.

keyTerms.meaning: He read about himself (applied the פסוק to himself)

steps.whatToRemember: The fat's red veins did not rot, which proved that רבי אלעזר judged correctly. He saw in himself the פסוק 'My flesh also dwells in safety.'

phrases.english: He read about himself:
"My flesh also dwells in safety."
phrases.notes: תהלים 16:9

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the story after the proof is confirmed
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: His flesh did not rot, a sign that he judged correctly, and he applied the פסוק to himself.

steps.title: A similar story begins with רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens a new story: the same kind of thing also happened to רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי.
steps.simpleTranslation: And a similar thing also came to רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up the next story. It tells us that רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי also had a similar experience, and the details come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word וְאַף, 'and also', ties this new story to the story of רבי אלעזר. That signals the same kind of situation is coming, now with a different חכם.

phrases.english: And also Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei
it came to (him)
phrases.notes: The sentence keeps going after this. It means the same kind of situation happened to him too.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאַף רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי מְטָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a parallel story after the רבי אלעזר story ends
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A similar situation also came to רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי.
